11.0.s.en: (1) The future of the Jews with regard to salvation

11.0.0.en: Although God described Israel as a stubborn people in the previous chapter, this does not mean at all that He closed the door of salvation to those among them who want to believe in Him. The proof is that St. Paul himself, an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin, was accepted by God when he responded to the love of Christ for him, and He brought him into the fold of faith, not only as a believer but as a great preacher.

11.1.0.en: God, who chose Israel as His people, cannot reject them, even after they crucified Him and rejected Him. Although He rejected them as a political state when He said, "Behold, your house is left unto you desolate" (Mt 23:38), announcing the end of the Jewish religion, He will remain always and forever with open arms toward everyone from the people of Israel who believes in Him. For in every generation there is a small Israelite remnant who believe in Him. The proof is that when the prophet Elijah complained to God about the people of Israel, saying that they had killed the prophets and torn down the altars (that is, they had replaced the worship of God with the worship of idols), and that they sought to kill Elijah himself, God answered that He had seven thousand men who had not bowed the knee to Baal (1 Kgs 19:18). The number seven signifies perfection and the number one thousand heavenly life, that is, the seven thousand live in the perfection of heavenly life, seeking not earthly things but heavenly things.

11.2.0.en: Likewise in the time of Paul, indeed in all times, there is a chosen Israelite remnant who enter into faith in Christ. How does this happen? By the election of grace, that is, God looks upon hearts and sees who is ready to receive Him, and sends him the grace of the Holy Spirit to support him, enlighten his heart and strengthen him to enter the Christian faith and be baptized, so that the Holy Spirit abides in him forever.

11.3.0.en: "No more of works": that is, the works of the Law.

11.3.1.en: "Otherwise grace is no more grace": grace would be of no benefit for salvation.

11.3.2.en: "But if it be of works, then is it no more grace": if salvation were by the works of the Law, it would not be by the grace of Christ, and the works of the Law would suffice us for salvation.

11.3.3.en: "Otherwise work is no more work": the works of the Law would no longer be a work that saves man, but rather a preparation for rejecting sin, so that we may believe in Christ and receive salvation by His grace.

11.3.4.en: St. Paul returns to affirm that their election is not based on the works of their law. For if their works were the cause of their salvation, they would have no need of the grace of God. And who can be saved without the grace of God?

11.4.0.en: Israel did not obtain salvation because it sought it, as though it were an absolute right that it deserved because it had worked by the Law. The elect among the Israelites obtained salvation through their humility and their reliance on the grace of Christ, but the rest, the proud and hard of heart, who rejected the despised, crucified Christ, did not obtain salvation.

11.5.0.en: When God found them hard of heart, He left them in their hardness and withheld His grace from them because they rejected it. When a person looks at them, he finds them as though in a deep sleep, neither hearing nor seeing. Behold, the world around them believes in Christ and receives salvation in every generation. Although they saw Christ and heard His teaching, they closed their hearts, eyes and ears to Him. This verse is a prophecy about them from both Moses the prophet (Deut 29:4) and Isaiah the prophet (Isa 29:10-12).

11.6.0.en: This verse is also a prophecy about them from David the prophet. The table signifies the Law, on which the Jews relied and with which alone they were satisfied, while rejecting Christ. This same Law will judge them, that is, it will be a snare and a ruin to them on the day of judgment. Thus St. Paul has called the prophets of the Jews, Moses, Isaiah and David, to witness against them in their rejection of faith in Christ.

11.7.0.en: That verse, from Ps 69:22-23, does not mean that the Apostle Paul is invoking blindness and a bowed back upon them. Rather, he wants to say that whoever wants blindness and a bowed back, that is, incapacity for spiritual work in spite of God's calling him, let it be to him as he wishes. The grace of God will no longer press upon him, but God will leave him, so that when he is wearied he may return to God and repent.

11.7.1.en: Note, beloved, that the table of the Old Testament is very rich, for it contains many symbols of the atoning work of Christ, but the Jews, sadly, took the words of the Law literally and did not understand that it is a symbol and a preparation for Christ.

11.7.2.en: Be ready at all times to learn from those around you, and do not let pride prevent you from being a disciple and from understanding God's messages to you on the lips of those around you. For humility is the way to knowledge, wisdom and all that is good.

11.8.s.en: (2) God's call to the Jews to believe in Christ

11.8.0.en: "Stumbled": they did not believe, trust and accept Christ the Savior.

11.8.1.en: "Fall": that God rejected them to the end.

11.8.2.en: "To provoke them to jealousy": that is, so that they may become zealous and turn to faith in Christ.

11.8.3.en: St. Paul asks a rhetorical question: does the Jews' unbelief that Jesus is the awaited Messiah, and their rejection of Him, mean that they have fallen utterly?

11.8.4.en: Certainly not, for their stumbling is a temporary period, so that when they turned away from faith, God turned to rescue the Gentiles. One of the benefits of this, perhaps, is to stir up a spirit of jealousy in the hearts of the Jews.

11.9.0.en: "Their fall": a temporary fall through their rejection of faith in Christ and His crucifixion.

11.9.1.en: "Their diminishing": their being empty of faith in Christ.

11.9.2.en: St. Paul returns to lift the spirits of the Jews, so he describes their condition as a "fall," just as he showed that God turned their fall to good by opening His arms to the Gentiles.

11.9.3.en: But the greatest joy will be at their fullness, that is, the return of the majority of them to faith in Christ, which will be a blessing for the whole world, for the material world will end and we will begin to enjoy the Kingdom of Heaven, and that will be at the end of the days.

11.10.0.en: Here he reassures the Gentiles that he was not distracted from them by serving the Jews, affirming that he is essentially an apostle to the Gentiles, and that this ministry must be glorified and bear more and more fruit.

11.11.0.en: Paul speaks in this manner in the hope that it may lead the Jews to be jealous of the glory that the Gentiles have received, and so believe.

11.12.0.en: When the Jews rejected the Lord Christ, the pagan half entered into faith. Therefore when the Jewish half returns to faith in Christ, the world, in both its Jewish and Gentile halves, will be in the faith; that is, the whole world will be raised from the death of sin and denial, enjoying the spiritual resurrection and in a state of reconciliation with God.

11.12.1.en: In sum, the Jews will return to the faith before the end of the world, and God awaits their return.

11.13.0.en: Now, what is the value of the Jews in God's sight? Here St. Paul likens the Fathers (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob) to the firstfruit (which is the offering of the first of the harvest to God, so that the whole wheat crop used for the dough is blessed by it), and likens the Jewish people to the holy lump itself. Then he returns to liken the Fathers to the root (the root and trunk of a good tree) and the Jewish people to the good branches of that tree.

11.14.0.en: But some dry branches came out of that tree, that is, the Jews who refused to believe, so God cut them off and cast them away. And you, O Gentile, are like a wild olive tree (which bears no fruit); God had compassion on you in His mercy and found in you a readiness to partake with the rich olive tree, so He grafted you into it, and you have become related to it and nourished by it.

11.15.0.en: Certainly you cannot boast against the broken-off branches, that is, the Jews who were rejected for their unbelief, thinking that you are better, even if you bear beautiful spiritual fruit. The glory, the boast and the credit go back to the root, that is, the fathers and prophets of the Jewish people, which bears you and nourishes you, and without which you would have fallen.

11.16.0.en: If you say in your heart, "I am the branch that stands, better than the original branches that were broken off, because God rejected them and put me in their place," then know the true reason for their fall, which is unbelief, and the true reason for your standing, which is your faith. This makes you not proud and boastful, but fearful of falling.

11.16.1.en: The fear of God is the way of your salvation, and your humility supports you. So examine yourself with repentance, knowing that you are less than all creatures, yet it is God who glorifies you with His love and His gifts. The more you fear God, the more you reject sin, so your heart is purified, you cling to His love, and you live for Him with all your heart.

11.17.0.en: For God's rule is that the unbeliever is cut off. If this rule applies without partiality to the natural branches, that is, the Jews who rejected Christ, what then of the grafted branches that are not original, that is, the Gentiles, if they do not abide in faith? Without doubt, if they reject faith they will perish.

11.18.0.en: God is kind to those who abide in faith, but He is severe and cuts off those who reject faith, who do not abide in it and who despise His kindness.

11.19.0.en: As for the natural branches that were cut off, that is, the Jews who rejected faith, God will graft them in again if they leave the state of unbelief in which they are, for God is able to draw them to faith.

11.20.0.en: Paul declares that the faith and return of the Jews who rejected it is not impossible, for if you, O Gentile, a wild olive tree different from the original olive tree, were grafted into it by God, how much more easily can God graft in the branches that have the same nature as the original olive tree, that is, the Jews when they repent.

11.20.1.en: For this reason the Church loved the books of the Old Testament and read them, and even took chapters from them for her Church readings, because it is the root of the olive tree. She looks to the Jews to return to the olive tree and come back to faith, since apart from faith they are like a dry, dead branch whose end is fire. The Lord Christ said to every person in (Jn 15:6), "If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned."

11.21.0.en: Here St. Paul sums up the truth that every Gentile must not forget: that Israel has been hardened in part, that is, some of the Jews rejected faith so that an opportunity might be given to the Gentiles to enter it. The Gentile should not think that the story ended at this point, lest he be ignorant of the wisdom of God, who will receive the Jews into the faith before the end of the days. This is a clear prophecy of the faith of the Jews at the end of the days. St. Paul called this event a mystery, because it is hard for the human mind to grasp that the Jews who crucified Christ will return to believe in Him after all these long years of denial.

11.22.0.en: How will Israel be saved? By the Deliverer, Jesus Christ, who works in hearts and changes them when they show readiness for that, and turns them away from their evils. And what is the greatest ungodliness? Is it not the denial of Christ?

11.23.0.en: In sum, God promises the return of Israel to the faith at the end of the days, when they leave their sins, that is, the hardness of their hearts, their rejection of Christ and all their evil desires.

11.24.0.en: The Jews are now considered enemies of the Gospel and of the preaching of it, until the preaching reaches the whole world. The Americas, for example, did not receive the preaching until the sixteenth century, and Africa in the twentieth century. Until faith reaches all the nations, that is, the fullness of the Gentiles (v. 25), the Jews will remain enemies of the Gospel. Then the Jews will return to faith because they are originally God's chosen people, and beloved of God for the sake of their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

11.25.0.en: These are the fathers to whom God promised that their descendants would remain His people, and God cannot go back on His promises and gifts.

11.25.1.en: The Jews have misunderstood these verses of St. Paul's epistle, and thought that he was prophesying to them the establishment of a state that usurps the rights of others in order to restore its former glory and revive its religion with its sacrifices and its temple. Of course St. Paul did not mean this, because Christianity does not tie believers to an earthly inheritance but to a heavenly kingdom that does not perish.

11.26.0.en: And you, O Gentiles, God called you from the beginning of humanity, but you rejected God's call while Abraham and his people accepted it. But now, after your repentance, you have become worthy of mercy, while the Jews disobeyed. But when the Jews repent and return to God at the end of the days, they will be shown mercy with the same kind of mercy that you were shown.

11.26.1.en: Perhaps these verses are a lesson to every person not to despise anyone, however great his sin. For who knows, perhaps that sinner today will be a great saint tomorrow.

11.27.0.en: For God first closed the door of mercy on the Gentiles because of their earlier disobedience to Christ, and then closed the door of mercy on the Jews because of their disobedience after the Incarnation of Christ. Then the door of mercy was opened to the Gentiles after they accepted Christ from the first century, and the door of mercy will be opened to the Jews before the Second Coming of Christ. So all, Gentiles and Jews, are equal in that they were rejected once and shown mercy once. Thus the mercy of Christ will come upon all, though at different times.

11.28.0.en: Truly, what a wondrous composition and what a wisdom beyond comprehension belongs to God! He directs all events so that they achieve their noble aims in the end. And what a great foreknowledge He has! Who can claim knowledge and say, "I can examine the judgments of God," as though he were greater than God, or who can investigate and search out God's ways and methods, as though God's plans lacked precision or wisdom?

11.29.0.en: Who can say, "I know how God thinks," or "I am God's counselor"?

11.30.0.en: Who gave God something of his own, as a man, and so deserved a reward for his gift to God? That is, what did Israel give God that it dares to demand its right, as though God were indebted to it?

11.31.0.en: "For of him" (God created all things), "and through him" (all things exist, live, are preserved and remain by His power and wisdom), "and to him" (all things are indebted to Him and work for His glory). In sum, God deserves all glory.

11.31.1.en: Finally, beloved, things may happen in your life that seem hard to understand and that the human mind cannot grasp now, but the great wisdom of God, which keeps and shepherds you, will be revealed to you one day, and then you will realize how much God loved you, and that all His plans and arrangements turned out for your good in the end, because He alone is the Maker of good things, the merciful and compassionate. So accept all that comes upon you and thank God for it, confident of His love and His fatherhood toward you.

11.31.2.en: Gifts and virtues, from chapter 12 to 16: the practical commandments in the Epistle to the Romans
